item.title: How will the victory by Germany’s far-right AfD in a state election affect the country’s politics?
item.description: There will be close scrutiny of the extent to which the party can implement its hard-right manifesto.
item.content:encoded:
The results of Germany’s Saxony-Anhalt state election on September 6 were far worse than feared for the country’s mainstream political parties. The far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) came close to winning a majority of votes, with 43.8%. This was about 4% higher than polls had suggested.

Support for the centre-right Christian Democratic Union of Germany (CDU), on the other hand, imploded. It won 17.2% of the vote, down from 37.1% in 2021, performing substantially worse than predicted.

At nearly 78%, turnout was up substantially compared with 2021 – in a way that helped the AfD. Analysis suggests the growth in its support came mostly from former non-voters, joined by a substantial number of erstwhile Christian Democratic Union of Germany supporters.

The polarised nature of the election, with 41% of voters surveyed beforehand wanting an AfD-led government but 46% favouring one led by the CDU, had some surprising effects. One was that it flattered the social democratic SPD and the Greens.

Both the SPD and Greens received tactical support from CDU and Left Party voters to make sure they reached the 5% of votes required to win seats in the state parliament.

item.title: William T Vollmann has written a 3,000‑page novel when the world appears to be done with big books
item.description: Vollmann’s new novel, ‘A Table for Fortune’, explores what happens when the response to the horrors of 9/11 becomes an arena for perpetration of more crimes.
item.content:encoded:
With forecasters of doom debating the end of reading, of publishing and of literacy in general, what should we make of William T Vollmann’s forthcoming novel, A Table for Fortune?

Spanning four volumes at 3,000 pages, is it madness? A determined attempt to silence print’s naysayers?

I have been writing about Vollmann’s works since I penned the introduction to “William T Vollmann: A Critical Companion” more than 10 years ago.

The 67-year-old author has spent his career going big, in every sense, and I would not be the first to describe his approach to his art as uncompromising.

His projects grapple with weighty matters such as global poverty, the history of North America and climate change. Few of his roughly 25 books run under 500 pages. About half try to keep his readers engaged for several hundred pages beyond that. Many of them supplement the text with photographs, epigraphs, glossaries, family trees, sketches, timelines, variant tables of contents, alternating fonts and notes to the reader. The essay “Rising Up and Rising Down,” his philosophical and journalistic inquiry into the nature of violence, clocks in at over 3,000 pages across seven volumes.

item.title: Delhi airport files FIR against 63 social media handles for ‘misleading’ posts about waterlogging
item.description: Water had temporarily accumulated in Terminal 3 arrival forecourt on September 4, but was cleared within 20 minutes, said the airport operator.
item.content:encoded:
The Delhi International Airport Limited said on Wednesday that it has filed a first information report against 63 social media handles for circulating allegedly misleading posts about flooding and waterlogging at the Indira Gandhi International Airport last week.

On September 4, water temporarily accumulated in the airport’s Terminal 3 arrival forecourt following heavy rainfall.

The “incorrect posts” had shown that the airport was flooded and falsely suggested that operations had been disrupted, the operator stated.

In one case, it said, an old video of waterlogging at Dubai Airport was shared as footage from Delhi.

Such content was “intended to create public mischief, spread misinformation, defame a critical public utility service and create unwarranted concerns among passengers”, said the airport operator.

It added that the area had received about 72.2 mm of rain between 2.30 pm and 5.30 pm on September 4, and that the accumulated water was cleared within 20 minutes without affecting airport operations.

Eleven flights were diverted between 3.30 pm and 5 pm on September 4 due to bad weather, The Indian Express reported. Five were diverted to Jaipur, four to Lucknow, and one each to Ahmedabad and Chandigarh.

The licence of an Indian Railway Catering and Tourism Corporation-linked kitchen in the city was also suspended after inspectors found live cockroaches in the food storage and processing areas. They also found that food was being prepared near open garbage, the newspaper reported.

The action came amid a statewide drive by the administration against eateries and other establishments for alleged violations of food safety norms.

The inspection at ISKCON’s Hare Krishna Land in Juhu was conducted on September 3. The inspectors found that the storage areas had rodent droppings and the drains were clogged with food waste.

At the main food establishment at the centre, the FDA found poor raw material checks, improper storage, pest infestation and inadequate cleaning and drainage, The Indian Express reported.

It also flagged that records for water testing, employee medical checks, vaccination, training and audits were missing.

item.title: Nepal floods halt contentious hydropower exports to Bangladesh via India
item.description: The disruption comes amid load-shedding in Bangladesh and a few months after an Indian power trading company declined Nepal’s request to export 20 MW more.
item.content:encoded:
Monsoon rains have routinely given Nepal a surge of hydropower, creating a surplus. Some of that surplus was used to supplement downstream neighbour Bangladesh’s fossil-fuel-dependent electricity supply.

On August 2, however, Nepal’s hydropower system was damaged extensively. Flash floods swept through the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river systems, killing at least 1,250 people as of 3 September. The floods also damaged 15 hydropower plants and critical transmission infrastructure, wiping out over 750 MW of electricity generation, reported Time. Nearly 900 hydropower workers are missing.

The disaster has now disrupted Nepal’s electricity exports, with supplies to Bangladesh halted, authorities in Dhaka and Kathmandu confirmed to Dialogue Earth.

On September 3, Shaligram Bhandari, a spokesperson for Nepal’s Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation, told Dialogue Earth that floods damaged the 22 megawatt Chilime and 24 MW Trishuli hydropower projects, which have since stopped generating electricity. The power they produced had been approved for export to Bangladesh. Nepal halted all power exports, Reuters reported several days earlier.

Amid the disaster, the ministry had yet to explore alternatives, Bhandari said. Nepal’s growing role as a hydropower exporter must be viewed together with these vulnerabilities.

item.description: An excerpt from ‘Wandered the Traveller’, by Nisar Aziz Butt, translated from the Urdu by Daisy Rockwell.
item.content:encoded:
Afgar had lost her parents so long ago she had no recollection of them at all. They’d had no time to enjoy their marriage and contemplate the joy of spending their lives together before they’d fallen prey to cholera and entrusted nine-month-old Afgar to her maternal grandmother. It was with this grandmother that she had lived when she was not being passed back and forth from house to house between her paternal uncles, paternal aunts and maternal aunts. She had no maternal uncles. When she was five, her grandmother passed on as well, leaving her care to the world. The events following her grandmother’s death were still vivid in her memory. She had no recollection of anything before that, just a handful of faint, meaningless images, whereas those incidents were clear in her mind. They were not particularly pleasant.

item.title: Why social media thinks government intentionally slowed internet after Delhi building collapse
item.description: So widespread was this belief that the Delhi Police had to ‘fact check’ it. But Modi government’s poor transparency record means that suspicion has lingered.
item.content:encoded:
On Monday, Harsh Mamnani, a Delhi-based independent video journalist, put out an unusual request on Instagram. He asked his followers where he could find high-speed internet in Satya Niketan, the South Delhi neighbourhood where a five-storey building used as paying guest accommodation by students had collapsed the previous day, killing at least seven people and injuring several others.

The 24-year-old, who has reported from the site of the collapse every day since Sunday, said he felt compelled to seek help because his mobile phone internet was simply too slow to upload videos. Mamnani thought this was because the government had slowed down the speed of mobile phone internet. “I am pretty sure they [the government] did it,” he asserted.

Student-activists who have visited the area frequently this week were also certain that “jammers” had been used on Sunday, the day the collapse occurred, as well as Monday. “The government did not want us to circulate videos because that could have led to a big protest,” alleged Sagar Suman, a PhD scholar from the Jawaharlal Nehru University who volunteers with the left-wing outfit, Disha Students’ Organisation.

item.title: Maharashtra SIR: 30% voters deleted in seats with higher Muslim population, says report
item.description: The state-level average is 21.1%, which amounts to more than two crore persons.
item.content:encoded:
Nearly 30% of voters in 38 Maharashtra Assembly constituencies, where Muslims account for more than one-fifth of the population, have been excluded from the draft lists published as part of the state's special intensive revision of electoral rolls, The Indian Express reported on Wednesday.

The enumeration forms of more than 37 lakh voters, or 29.7% of the previous electoral base, have been marked as “uncollectable” in the 38 constituencies. The state-level average is 21.1%, which amounts to more than two crore persons.

The 29 constituencies reserved for the Scheduled Castes had an average exclusion rate of 19.6%, The Indian Express reported. The 25 seats reserved for Scheduled Tribes had an average exclusion rate of 13.2%.

The “uncollectables”, or those removed from the draft voter list, have been marked as either permanently shifted, deceased, absent, duplicate entries or placed under the “other” category, which includes those who refused to fill the enumeration form.

The deletions pattern

The highest rates of deletions have been recorded in densely populated constituencies. Pune district had the highest number of deletions at 28.6 lakh, followed by Thane with 28.5 lakh and Mumbai Suburban with 26.5 lakh, data from the Election Commission showed.

In Mumbai Metropolitan Region’s Bhiwandi East, 49.1% of voters have been removed, followed by Bhiwandi West at 44.7% and Kalwa-Mumbra at 42.9%, reported The Indian Express.

On September 1, the Supreme Court ordered that all first information reports registered across the country in connection with student protests held between July 20 and July 25 should not be pursued or investigated and must be treated as closed, except those involving people with criminal antecedents. “Then what was the point?” she asked her school uniform. The uniform didn’t reply, but it looked a bit crushed, too.

“Idea!” Saru squealed midway through breakfast. “I’ll type out a sorry message! You’ll forward it to everyone?” She looked up at her older sister. Sadly, Taru Didi was looking down at her phone, as usual. Saru’s face fell. Taru Didi had no time for her these days. item.description: The court said that decision on Dara Singh’s remission plea had been adjourned repeatedly for nearly two years.
item.content:encoded:
The Supreme Court on Tuesday criticised the Odisha government for failing to decide on the premature release of Bajrang Dal member Dara Singh, who is serving a life sentence for the 1999 murder of Australian missionary Graham Staines and his two sons, Live Law reported.

On August 19, the bench had given the Odisha Sentence Review Board a final opportunity and verbally stated that the court would take the decision in the matter if the state failed to do so by the next hearing.

However, counsel for the Odisha government on Tuesday sought a four-week adjournment, citing the illness of its advocate-on-record, the legal news outlet reported.

Staines and his minor sons were burnt to death by a mob led by Singh in Odisha in January 1999 when they were sleeping in a jeep. The attackers had accused the missionary of illegal religious conversion.

Singh was among the 14 persons convicted in 2003 by a special Central Bureau of Investigation court. He was sentenced to death by the CBI court, but the sentence was commuted to life imprisonment in 2005 by the Orissa High Court.

item.title: ‘It could kill us all’: Anthropic researcher quits over AI safety concerns
item.description: The artificial intelligence industry was ‘racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives’, Jacob Coxon said on social media.
item.content:encoded:
A researcher at artificial intelligence company Anthropic has quit, claiming that he is concerned that the firm and the industry are racing to build AI systems that he believes they will not be able to control.

In a series of social media posts on Wednesday, Jacob Coxon said that he had done pre-training research at United States-based firms Anthropic and OpenAI for the past three years, and that “neither company is acting responsibly”. The firms were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives”, he said.

In AI, “pre-training” refers to the initial phase where a machine learning model learns patterns, grammar, facts and structures from a dataset before it can be trained for specific tasks.

In a series of social media posts, Coxon said that people should not underestimate the power of artificial intelligence.

“These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionise any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources,” he said. “We have all witnessed the progress in each of these domains, and progress is not slowing.”

Anthropic has not yet commented on Coxon’s resignation, or on the concerns he raised.

item.title: Instead of chasing GDP growth, India must redesign its broken ladder of upward mobility
item.description: Young Indians only want gainful employment to secure their future. The economy has simply not delivered on that.
item.content:encoded:
India’s leaders must find systemic solutions to the country’s employment problems. The economy is not creating enough good jobs for young people, even if more were to pursue higher education and the examination system functioned smoothly. More technology to fix the examination system will not solve the deeper problem of the economy.

Moreover, there is increasing evidence that use of more technology and AI will worsen India’s unemployment crisis. item.title: Can you teach yourself to detect AI writing? Maybe

item.content:encoded:
AI is quietly reshaping writing. It’s not just that prose is changing – the very structure of written language is genuinely changing too.

It’s not just a new technology.

It’s not a fad.

It’s an undeniable revolution.

Did this article’s introduction seem AI-generated? What made you feel that way?

The truth is, it was not AI-generated; I wrote it to emulate synthetic prose, the kind you get when a large language model (LLM) organises words into text.

That kind of prose suddenly seems to be everywhere: on low-quality websites built to accumulate advertising clicks, in social media captions chasing engagement, and even book manuscripts. Crime novelist Jerry Falade recently lost a book deal worth more than $2 million after his literary agents said they could no longer faithfully determine how his manuscript had come together. Hachette pulled the horror novel Shy Girl in March this year under similar suspicion.

Chief Justice Surya Kant questioned the panel’s request for time till February 28 to submit its conclusions, asking whether it was waiting for his retirement.

The committee, formed in May, was tasked with defining the Aravallis after the Supreme Court’s adoption of a definition by a Union environment ministry panel led to widespread protests, particularly in Rajasthan. item.title: Why do people respond differently to mosquito bites? A scientist explains
item.description: The reaction reflects a complex interaction between mosquito saliva and the immune system.
item.content:encoded:
Two people spend an evening in the same garden and receive roughly the same number of mosquito bites. By morning, one barely notices them – while the other is covered in large, swollen, intensely itchy welts that linger for days.

Most of us have experienced this, or know someone who has. But why is it that mosquito bites affect some people so differently? The answer lies in the way a mosquito’s saliva interacts with our unique immune system.

When a mosquito bites you, they inject saliva into your skin. The immune system recognises the saliva as foreign and releases histamine – an immune cell chemical that causes allergy symptoms such as redness, swelling and itchiness.

But this only partly explains what’s going on. A mosquito’s saliva also contains a range of other biologically active compounds that interact with the immune system in more complex ways than once assumed.

For instance, a mosquito’s saliva also contains proteins that prevent blood clotting and keep blood flowing so they can feed undisturbed.

These same salivary proteins influence the immune response that occurs at the bite site. Rather than acting solely as a feeding aid, mosquito saliva can alter the local immune environment within minutes of a bite.

When Osama Manzar started the nonprofit Digital Empowerment Foundation in 2002, just 1.2% of India’s population was online. Now, more than 70% is. But Manzar’s mission statement – helping poor and rural communities come out of the digital dark to access information, literacy, and livelihoods – still holds.

In the age of artificial intelligence, Manzar senses the risk of another extractive technology, with the benefits and control concentrated among powerful actors both at the algorithmic level and in terms of land and water.

item.title: Long gaps between meals affect older people differently, shows study
item.description: Ageing changes how people digest food, absorb nutrients, control blood sugar and maintain muscle.
item.content:encoded:
Going for much of the day without eating is often promoted as a way to improve health or lose weight. But a new study suggests that long gaps between meals may have different effects on older adults – especially those in the oldest age groups.

For the study, my colleagues and I followed nearly 3,000 people aged 60 and over in Sweden and found that those who usually went longest without eating developed chronic diseases faster than those who had shorter gaps between meals. The difference was clearest among people aged 78 and over.

This does not mean that fasting causes disease in old age, nor that every older person should avoid long intervals without food. But it does raise questions about whether advice based on studies of younger and middle-aged adults can be safely applied to older age groups.

Fasting helps the body switch from using readily available sugar to using stored energy, such as fat. Studies in younger adults have linked some forms of fasting to better control of blood sugar and other potentially beneficial changes in metabolism. item.title: In a surprising reversal of trends, world’s mangrove forests are expanding
item.description: What’s driving this? And could it help curb climate change?
item.content:encoded:
Mangroves are perplexing plants.

They breathe through their roots, appear to stand on stilts and grow best in hot, salty seawater drawn in and out by the tide.

Historically, mangrove forests have been dismissed as inhospitable places to avoid and have been extensively cleared. But these fascinating trees are now gaining attention for how they support biodiversity, store carbon and buffer the effects of storms, cyclones and tsunamis.

Since 1984, scientists have been monitoring the growth and geographical reach of mangrove forests using satellites. And for the first time, these unique ecosystems are expanding at a faster rate than they are declining.

So what’s driving this? And could it help curb climate change?

Why mangroves matter

Mangrove forests were long viewed as largely expendable places. Research shows people were quick to convert them into rice paddies, oil palm plantations and aquaculture operations. Some were even used as rubbish tips.

However, mangrove forests are now recognised as a vital part of our coastal environments. They provide habitat for a wealth of plants and animals including fish such as barramundi and giant shovelnose rays, reptiles such as seasnakes and even mammals such as the proboscis monkey and water mouse. They are crucial carbon stores, locking up roughly four times more carbon than other land-based forests. Mangroves can also shelter coastal communities and ecosystems from natural disasters by reducing the risk of flooding and erosion.

item.title: ‘The Grave Exhumers and Other Stories’: A close-up of Muslim lives outside Kolkata’s urban premises

The stories in The Grave Exhumers and Other Stories by Lutfor Rahaman were written when he was 21 years old. To be 21 and have such a deep-rooted grasp of the colour, habitation, geography, and taste of the air is remarkable to witness. And what’s more impressive is the fact that translator Mursed Alam has managed to get these details and idiosyncrasies without diluting them.

Comprising six short stories, the collection zeroes down on death in some or the other form. For instance, even a seemingly optimistic story (at least by the title) called “Collectors of Hope”, starts thus: “Sohrab lost the job, finally!”

item.title: Dolly Parton and Gloria Steinem: Two ways to fight for women’s freedoms

Two legends passed away in this past month – Dolly Parton and Gloria Steinem. While each has a distinct and vastly different persona, I see them both as pioneers of women’s rights and freedoms. Each did a great deal in entirely different ways to advance women’s rights and both were known far beyond America.

Dolly was not driven by a scripted feminist ideology nor did she preach it – she lived the life of a liberated woman defying stereotypes of what women should look, sound like, be and do.

The duo behind the criminally underrated Dungeons & Dragons: Honor Among Thieves ensure a safe landing for Mayday. Written and directed by Jonathan Goldstein and John Francis Daley, Mayday is an American-Russian bhai-bhai movie starring Ryan Reynolds, Kenneth Branagh and the Tom Cruise hit Top Gun.

It’s 1987, a year after the release of Top Gun – a pop culture milestone as far as Mayday is concerned. The Cold War between the United States of America and the former Soviet Union is still in place.

US Navy pilot Troy (Reynolds) is a vocal supporter of his country’s foreign policy and military might. Russia is the Bad Guy, with no democracy and a submissive populace, Troy firmly believes. Until he crash-lands in Russia during an intelligence-gathering mission and is rescued by former KGB operative Nikolai (Branagh).

item.title: September Indian fiction: Six new titles (including Amit Chaudhuri’s) to look forward to
item.description: A Telugu novel in translation set during the Emergency, a debut collection of short stories from Manipur, a historical fiction from World War One, and more.
item.content:encoded:

Château Rouge, Amit Chaudhuri

A writer is invited to Paris and finds himself living in an area that bears little resemblance to his idea of the city. With the passing of time, his disquiet translates into a way of seeking and experiencing a truer, more unlikely Paris.

Château Rouge takes up residence in that area before floating freely through the city. It takes its time, exploring tangents, diversions, side streets, creeping into new spaces and remote angles, to open up fresh ground and appraise the city, the experience of travel, otherness – and the novel itself – anew.

The Imitation Englishman, Devki Pande

It is 1916, and the First World War is raging across Europe. Madhusudan Chandra Joshi is a young Indian clerk working at the District Courts when he travels to Heidelberg to study law. There, a chance encounter with the mysterious revolutionary Amir Farooqui changes the course of his life.

item.title: ‘Writing should be a calling ideally, not an escape hatch’: Novelist and poet Meena Kandasamy
item.description: ‘Books are not an outdated format if they are done right. They become outdated when they have nothing new to offer.’
item.content:encoded:
Meena Kandasamy took the literary world by storm with her first collection of poetry, Touch, in 2006. Two decades hence, her novel Fieldwork as a Sex Object is out. Her other books include Ms Militancy, a book of poems that take on the pretensions of a valorised mythology; and The Orders Were to Rape You, a work that documents the lives of women who gave everything to the Tamil Eelam struggle.

Her novel When I Hit You was shortlisted for the 2018 Women’s Prize.

In a conversation with publisher S Anand of Navayana, Kandasamy spoke about cancel culture, why social media feels so essential to modern existence, and how her parents shaped her as a writer.

Recent developments regarding abusive literary “greats” recall the oft-cited directive to separate the art from the artist. How has this aged today? Is it possible to judge the literary merits of a novel when its authors are known to be bad people?
Pablo Neruda, Pablo Picasso, Anne Sexton – almost every favourite of mine has had a fall from grace. I do not know how to quite answer this question. item.title: Ramachandra Guha: For 120 years, Indian students have fought to change politics and public life
item.description: A short history of student movements, from the swadeshi agitation in Bengal to the Cockroach Janta Party-led protests.
item.content:encoded:
In early July, as the students’ protests in Jantar Mantar were taking shape, the Trinamool Congress MP, Mahua Moitra, was one of the first politicians to show up in person and offer solidarity. Three weeks later, when the Union education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, resigned, Moitra thanked the younger generation “for saving Indian democracy” by bringing “this fascist, arrogant government to its knees”.

This, as she pointed out, was something the Opposition parties had not been able to do in the past 12 years.

Mahua Moitra’s praise was well merited. The resignation of the education minister, the home minister’s prolonged absence from Parliament, the sacking of several senior BJP office-bearers, and – not least – the clumsy, late-night videos of the prime minister, all testified to a regime whose customary air of hubristic arrogance had (at least temporarily) given way to weakness and confusion

item.title: Consumers can’t get enough pistachio – but concerns about its environmental impact are growing
item.description: The crop has a large carbon footprint and is worryingly water-intensive.
item.content:encoded:
Pistachio production has more than trebled in the last 20 years. In 2024, more than 1.4 million tonnes were produced globally. Their popularity has only increased in the last two years, with a growing status as a trendy, luxury food item.

However, this rise in popularity has come with concerns around the pistachio’s environmental impacts. There are also questions around whether their production can withstand changing climate conditions.

Pistachios originated in modern-day Turkey and Iran. Despite being considered a nut, they are actually the seeds of pistachio trees. These trees thrive in a hot summer climate but require relatively cold winter temperatures to ensure the trees flower at the right time in spring. They also require dry conditions, as high humidity can reduce yields and leave the trees susceptible to fungal disease.

In the late 19th and early 20th century, pistachios were popularised in the US by migrants from the Middle East. By the 1930s, pistachio orchards were established in California. The warm, dry climate of California provided ideal conditions for pistachio trees, so much so that the US has now overtaken Iran and Turkey as the world’s largest producer of pistachios.

item.title: ‘The Anniversary’: This Italian novel examines a patriarchal nuclear family and its links to fascism
item.description: A post-traumatic memoir of survival in which the narrator calmly recalls the turbulence of the past.
item.content:encoded:
Andrea Bajani’s novel, the winner of the 2025 Strega Prize, is a radical exploration of the psychology of family estrangement. It appears at a cultural moment where therapy-oriented language such as “gaslighting”, “boundaries”, and “toxic” has percolated into the most intimate realms of daily life and adult children are fearlessly breaking taboos and going no-contact with their parents by denouncing the abuse within highly dysfunctional households. The Anniversary examines the social institution of the patriarchal nuclear family and its links to fascism in Italy, showing how domestic violence and coercive control by male members of the family are rendered invisible and normative.

The totalitarian infrastructures

In the novel, following a series of “unreliable memories”, the narrator recalls events that led to the final goodbye with his parents ten years ago. With the dysfunctional family at its centre, The Anniversary is an intensely psychological novel. Yet it does not treat the trauma of upbringing as a problem that can be solved through psychoanalysis. Instead, it moves outward to reflect on wider social conditions that allow totalitarian values to be reproduced in the private realms of the modern nuclear family.

item.title: Has El Niño’s monsoon effect hit India’s kharif crops?
item.description: Former Union agriculture secretary Siraj Hussain says there is unlikely to be any significant loss of foodgrain production despite the rain deficit.
item.content:encoded:
The threat of a strong El Niño still looming, rainfall in this year’s monsoon season varied by the month. June was one of the driest in India’s history, closing at a 35% deficit whereas July was 1% above normal.

This “normal” rainfall in July was largely driven by Central India whereas East and South India had a large deficit. As of August 26, the all India seasonal rainfall stands at a 13% deficit, in keeping with the weather agency’s forecast of a below-normal monsoon. The deficit is still most pronounced in East and South India.

There have also been floods or flood-like situations in Assam, Himachal Pradesh, and parts of the National Capital Region, Uttar Pradesh etc. What does this mean for India’s primary cropping season, that is, Kharif? What does this mean for farmers, foodgrain production, food prices and ultimately, for consumers?

Reviewing preparedness for this Kharif crop season earlier in June, Union agriculture minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan had said, “There is no need to panic. What is required is preparedness and collective action.”

Parish Priest-in-Charge Father Samuel Hembrom of St Claret Church told the newspaper that the mob forced the body, which had already been lowered into the grave, to be taken out. The body was later taken to another cemetery in Bardhaman town, he said.

item.title: ‘Da’: A novel about a child’s observation of queer lives has its heart in the right place
item.description: Author Arathi Menon situates the novel’s political concerns in her 13-year-old protagonist’s own coming-of-age story.
item.content:encoded:
I held on tightly to the page when 13-year-old Ved is asked, “Do you think gay people should go to jail?” As though a child’s answer could change lives. In Arathi Menon’s novel Da, this question follows the reader with a sense of urgency. In 2013, as the courts debated the rights of queer Indians, the reader turns to the child in hope. Menon writes of those turbulent times, from the eyes of a young boy, with great vulnerability and hope.

At the outset, the novel is described as a politically charged story on laws around homosexuality in India and its resultant stigma. I went into it expecting great tragedy and suffering. However, two chapters in and I was surprised by the notoriously inquisitive voice of an adolescent boy being brought up by his dead mother’s brother.

Ved is bright and thinks a lot and thereby talks a lot. I was reminded of nine-year-old Mira from Bhavika Govil’s 2025 novel Hot Water; a stunningly written voice of a young girl watching her dysfunctional family. Mira would make good friends with Ved. item.description: The demolition came after a complaint by former Bajrang Dal office bearer, who alleged that the structure had been illegally built within the DM office complex.
item.content:encoded:
The authorities in Uttar Pradesh on Saturday demolished a mosque situated within the Saharanpur district magistrate’s office complex, The Times of India reported. The demolition followed a court’s decision to uphold an earlier order declaring the structure illegal.

Samajwadi Party MP Iqra Hasan alleged that she was placed under house arrest by police at her Kairana residence to prevent her from travelling to Saharanpur, ANI reported.

The demolition followed a complaint by a former office bearer of the Bajrang Dal, who alleged that the mosque had been illegally constructed inside the district magistrate office complex, a sensitive government premises where confidential administrative work is conducted, The Times of India reported.

The Bajrang Dal and the Vishva Hindu Parishad are part of a group of Hindutva outfits led by the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, the parent organisation of the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party.

On July 17, the city magistrate’s court ordered the mosque’s demolition and directed its occupants to pay around Rs 6.41 crore as compensation, citing alleged encroachment and unauthorised use of government land.
